passage:
Tuesday. In the art period, Maria yanked the blue crayon out of Arohi's hand so hard that Arohi's drawing of her grandmother's house tore right through the roof. Arohi cried. Maria said, "It was already torn," and went back to her own page, but she couldn't colour anything properly all afternoon.
Wednesday. Maria waited by Arohi's bench before assembly. "I tore it. I'm sorry. I was mean about the crayon." She held out a roll of clear tape and a fresh sheet. They taped the roof from the back, and Maria redrew the chimney, very carefully.
Friday. At break Arohi called, "Maria, you're on my team!" and Maria ran over, lighter than she had felt all week.

qa.q: What did Maria bring to Arohi on Wednesday?
qa.a: She brought a roll of clear tape and a fresh sheet.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling on Tuesday afternoon after making her excuse?
qa.a: She felt guilty and uneasy, which is why she couldn't colour anything properly even though she had said it was already torn.

qa.q: Which choice helped Maria feel better, and why?
qa.a: Owning the tear and helping fix the drawing, because real repair eased her guilt in a way the excuse never did.

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt when Maria redrew the chimney?
qa.a: She probably felt cared for and ready to forgive, which is why she picked Maria for her team on Friday.

grounding: Shows a child who hurt a friend apologising and helping repair the harm, and then feeling free to play again.

passage:
"Lalremsiami, you've skipped choir three times now."
"I can't go back, Ira. Not after what I said."
"To Mawii? That was Saturday."
"I told her she sings like a door hinge. In front of everyone. I hear it every night. I heard it in the shower today."
"Have you said sorry?"
"How can I? Every time I picture her face I feel sick. I don't deserve to just walk back in."
Irawati sat down beside her on the hostel steps. "So you're punishing yourself by hiding. And Mawii still thinks you meant it."
Siami went quiet. "I thought feeling terrible was the sorry."
"It isn't. It's just terrible. The sorry is the part she actually hears."
"...Will you come with me tomorrow?"
"Yes. Before practice."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say to Mawii?
qa.a: She told Mawii she sings like a door hinge, in front of everyone.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami's replaying of the remark suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She feels deeply ashamed and sick with guilt, so much that she hides from choir rather than face Mawii.

qa.q: What next step did Irawati point Lalremsiami toward?
qa.a: Saying sorry to Mawii directly, since feeling terrible in private never reaches her; going together before practice makes it easier.

qa.q: What might Mawii think while Lalremsiami stays away?
qa.a: Mawii may still believe the remark was meant and feel hurt that no apology has come.

grounding: Shows a teenager replaying a harsh remark for days and mistaking private shame and avoidance for accountability.

passage: You want to know why I stopped arguing with Pema? I'm Nazia, his lab partner since first year, so I've heard it all. When he borrowed Tenzin's scooter and scraped it, it was the gravel's fault. When our group missed the project deadline because his part never came, it was the Wi-Fi. When he forgot Dechen's birthday, it was "you didn't remind me". Every time: "Not my fault." The funny thing is, he keeps bringing these things up. Late at night he'll say, "Tenzin's still weird with me, no?" So it clearly sits on him. Last week I just asked, "What was your part in it?" He was quiet so long I thought he'd hung up. Then he said, "I rode too fast." First time I've ever heard him say that. I think it was a relief for him.

qa.q: What did Pema blame for the scraped scooter?
qa.a: Pema said it was the gravel's fault.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Pema kept bringing up Tenzin?
qa.a: Nazia felt puzzled and a little frustrated, noticing that the guilt clearly still weighed on him despite all the excuses.

qa.q: Why did Nazia's question work better than arguing?
qa.a: Asking about his part invited Pema to own the harm himself, the step his excuses had always skipped.

qa.q: How might Pema feel after saying "I rode too fast"?
qa.a: He might feel exposed but lighter, since owning the harm finally gives the guilt somewhere to go.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing that someone's constant excuses leave his guilt unresolved until he finally owns his part.

passage: The scholarship form had sat on Nandini's desk in the Pune paying-guest room for eleven days. Maria picked it up. "Deadline's Friday. Why haven't you filled it?" "Because I wasted all of last year," Nandini said. "Skipped classes, slept till noon, failed two papers. People like me don't get to ask for things." Maria sat down on the bed. "You were nineteen and your dad had just moved away for work. What did you know then about handling that?" "Nothing," Nandini said slowly. "I didn't even know how to ask anyone for help." "So that girl did what she knew. You know more now." Nandini stared at the form for a long moment. Then she uncapped a pen and started on page one, hearing the old voice that said she hadn't earned it, and writing anyway.

qa.q: How long had the scholarship form sat on Nandini's desk?
qa.a: It had sat there for eleven days.

qa.q: Why hadn't Nandini filled in the form?
qa.a: She felt ashamed of wasting last year and believed she didn't deserve to ask for anything, so she kept punishing herself.

qa.q: Which question from Maria helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking what Nandini knew back then about handling it helped her see that her past self did what it could, so she could forgive it and act now.

qa.q: How might Maria see the old version of Nandini?
qa.a: Maria sees a nineteen-year-old struggling after a big change at home, not someone who should lose chances forever.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps punishing herself for a wasted year beginning to see that her past self did what it knew.

passage: On the bus home through Lagos traffic, Ada replayed the meeting: the load figure she had copied wrong, her manager's frown, the redo that cost the team two days. Her first thought was the usual one. Stupid. Careless. You'll never be good at this. Then she remembered what she had told Abebe last month when he failed his licensing exam: "You studied every night for months. You got one section wrong. Find out which and fix it." She took out her notebook and wrote to herself the way she had talked to him. "Ada, you copied one number wrong. You were rushing because you stayed late helping on the other file. Next time: check the figures before sending." She read it twice. Her shoulders came down from her ears. Tomorrow she would ask her manager for a second check on big numbers.

qa.q: What mistake did Ada make at work?
qa.a: She copied a load figure wrong.

qa.q: How did Ada feel after writing to herself the way she had talked to Abebe?
qa.a: She felt calmer and relieved; her shoulders came down from her ears.

qa.q: What made Ada's note to herself useful and not just kind?
qa.a: It named the exact error, why she was rushing and one fix to try, so it pointed toward change rather than only comfort.

qa.q: What would change if Ada kept calling herself stupid?
qa.a: She would probably feel worse and more afraid of mistakes, and be less likely to ask for the second check that could prevent the next one.

grounding: Shows a young adult after a work mistake speaking to herself as she would to a friend, naming both the error and the effort.

passage: Kalyani packed her own bag the night before: a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll. "Tomorrow we go to the mango grove, and it will be sunny," she told the goat. In the morning the village sky was grey, and big drops tapped the tin roof. Kalyani's face crumpled. "You said!" Her mother, Ganga, knelt down. "I said picnic. Picnic we'll have." She spread the mat on the verandah and set out the laddoos. Kalyani ate, watching the rain. "Tomorrow the grove?" "If the sky lets us." Kalyani nodded, sure again.

qa.q: What did Kalyani pack in her bag?
qa.a: She packed a steel tumbler, two groundnut laddoos and her cloth doll.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when the rain came?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and let down 😔 Her face crumpled as she said, "You said!"

qa.q: What did Ganga do that kept Kalyani's trust?
qa.a: She kept the part she had promised by holding the picnic on the verandah, and was careful to say "If the sky lets us" about tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Ganga had simply said, "No picnic today"?
qa.a: Kalyani might feel the promise was broken and trust tomorrow's plans a little less.

grounding: Shows a young child sure that tomorrow's picnic will be sunny, and a parent keeping the promise so that simple hope stays safe.

passage:
Wednesday night
Disha's diary. Spelling test on Friday. Last time I got 6 out of 15 and Ma'am wrote "Practise!" in red. This week Gurleen from next door tests me every evening on her steps. Monday I got 8. Tuesday 11. Today 13! "Necessary" and "rhythm" still beat me. I think I can get 14 on Friday, maybe all 15 if I learn those two. So tonight I wrote them ten times each and made up tricks: rhythm has two h's hiding like ears, and necessary has one collar and two sleeves. I'm not just wishing anymore. I can see the numbers going up. I'm going to ask Gurleen for one more round tomorrow before school.

qa.q: What did Disha score in today's test with Gurleen?
qa.a: Disha got 13.

qa.q: How is Disha feeling about Friday's test?
qa.a: Disha feels hopeful and determined 🙂 because the scores keep rising and there is a plan for the last two words.

qa.q: How could Gurleen support Disha before Friday?
qa.a: She could test just the two hard words in tomorrow's round and point out how far the scores have come since Monday.

qa.q: What might Gurleen feel seeing the scores rise each evening?
qa.a: Gurleen probably feels proud and pleased that the testing on her steps is helping.

grounding: Shows a child whose hope for a spelling test is tied to practice that visibly works, which keeps the effort going.

passage:
Subject: About the pre-board result
Yogesh Sir,
I got 23 in maths. You probably know already. I'm writing because I don't think I should come to Saturday class anymore. There's no point. If I can't pass the pre-board, I'll fail the board, and then no science, and then nothing I planned will happen. Everyone else seems to get it. I've tried, and it doesn't change.
I was going to stop there. But after class on Tuesday you said, "Bring me the paper, and we'll find the three chapters that cost you the most." I looked at it tonight. Most marks went in trigonometry and two word problems. That's three things, not everything.
Maybe I'll come on Saturday. Only to show you the paper.
Noor

qa.q: What score did Noor get in maths?
qa.a: Noor got 23.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling when starting the email?
qa.a: Noor felt hopeless and defeated, sure that failing the pre-board meant nothing planned would ever happen.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh Sir's suggestion help?
qa.a: It turned "everything is ruined" into a concrete task, finding the three chapters that cost the most, which Noor could actually do.

qa.q: How might Yogesh Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Yogesh Sir would probably feel concerned at first, then encouraged that Noor looked at the paper and might come on Saturday.

grounding: Shows a teenager's hope collapsing after a failed exam and widening again when a teacher offers one concrete next step.

passage:
Thursday
Sonali's diary. Parveen didn't come to lunch, so I found her behind the library, knees up, not crying, just staring. Her abbu's shop is closing and they're moving to her uncle's town in June. "Everything's finished," she said. "My friends, school, all of it." I almost said "It'll be fine!" but it won't be, not all of it, and she'd know I was lying. So I just sat. I didn't talk. After a long time she told me about the new school, and that her ammi cries in the kitchen at night. I asked what one thing would make June less scary. She said, "Knowing when I'd see you." So we made a plan: first holidays, she visits. I walked her home, and her ammi came to the gate and hugged her. Parveen said she'd talk to her ammi properly tonight.

qa.q: Where did Sonali find Parveen?
qa.a: Behind the library, sitting with her knees up.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stop before saying "It'll be fine!"?
qa.a: Sonali felt it would be dishonest, since not all of it would be fine, and was worried Parveen would know it was a lie.

qa.q: Which part of Sonali's response helped most?
qa.a: Sitting quietly and then asking about one thing that would make June less scary, which led to a real plan instead of empty cheer.

qa.q: What was it like for Parveen to have Sonali just sit with her?
qa.a: She probably felt less alone and safe enough to talk about the new school and her ammi crying at night.

grounding: Shows a friend answering another's despair by staying, listening and finding one small next step instead of promising everything will be fine.

passage: The power went out in the Siliguri hostel at 10:40 pm, and the application for the hotel management trainee post closed at midnight. Dolma's laptop showed 14%. It was her twenty-sixth application this month. Nineteen had never answered; four had said no. Her roommate Sonali held up a phone torch. "Why bother? They'll probably reject it anyway." "Probably," Dolma said, typing fast. "But definitely, if I don't send it." She cut the cover letter to two paragraphs to save battery, attached the certificate she had scanned that morning, and pressed submit at 11:52 with 3% left. Then she opened her notebook, drew a line under number twenty-six, and wrote twenty-seven: the airport lounge job, closes Monday.

qa.q: At what time did Dolma press submit?
qa.a: At 11:52, with 3% battery left.

qa.q: What does Dolma's reply "But definitely, if I don't send it" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels realistic and determined, accepting that rejection is likely but still hopeful enough to act.

qa.q: Which choice helped Dolma beat the power cut?
qa.a: Cutting the cover letter to two paragraphs saved battery and time, so the application still went in before midnight.

qa.q: How might Sonali see Dolma writing number twenty-seven?
qa.a: Sonali may feel puzzled or impressed, seeing Dolma keep going after so many silences instead of waiting for luck.

grounding: Shows a young adult who keeps applying for jobs despite likely rejections, acting with hope but without any guarantee.
